title: Inside the creator economy’s AI reckoning
content:
Few phenomena within the creator economy have moved as fast as AI’s embrace. What was once treated with anxious suspicion is now more widely viewed as a necessary strategy.
Last year, according to Kameron Buckner , founder of Social Docket , which helps creators navigate the legal implications of their work, the conversation around AI was defined by dread. This year, she says, the tone has shifted from fear to leverage — less “this thing is going to take over” and more how do we actually use it.
I spent the last several weeks talking to Buckner and others closest to this shift: top creators, consultants, founders, and social media strategists. Unsurprisingly, those who returned from the Cannes Lions International Festival of Creativity this year said AI was a centerpiece of the discourse.
But across the board, I sensed no real fear. Everyone I spoke to is using AI. Some more than others, some with discernment, others with keen enthusiasm. What’s certain is that AI has brought new questions to an industry built on areas like increasing productivity, monetizing creativity, and protecting IP. The bottom line: using it wisely is the difference between staying ahead of the curve and getting drowned out by it.
DonYé Taylor has been the mastermind behind culture-shifting campaigns and marketing strategies for brands like LVRN, Amazon, Nike, and Essence. She now runs her own functional-philosophy-meets-interior-design brand, Nuclei, alongside her newsletter, Mentally I’m Here. She believes AI doesn’t stand a chance against the ideas floating in her own brain — like one of her latest products, fittingly called the Brain Bank.
“AI is like a calculator,” says Taylor. “Just because I have a TI-89 doesn’t mean I’m going to get the right answer. I still need to put the right inputs into the calculator.”
Alicia Richardson , head of community and brand partnerships at FiveTwoNine and the founder of Black Create Connect, shares this sentiment. “It can enhance your creativity,” she says. “It doesn’t create your creativity. When it comes to raw, creator-led work specifically, she doesn’t think AI is ever going to take over, because audiences connect to people, not outputs.
Buckner tells her clients to think of AI less like a finished product and more like a running start. “Why start from a blank sheet of paper when you can start from an outline?” she says. In her own daily practice, prompting AI well has made her a better manager of actual human beings, because it forces her to get precise about what she wants before she asks for it. She applies that same instinct to her own visibility as a founder, using HubSpot’s AEO tool to check whether Social Docket shows up when someone searches for creator contract tools.
Gigi Robinson , a content creator and founder of the social media consulting business Hosts of Influence, works with her team to feed 15-plus minutes of raw footage into AI video tools to get a rough cut before a human editor touches it. The software finds the “book-worthy” moments, but a person still decides what makes the final edit. The payoff shows up in her numbers, too: Robinson estimates AI saves her more than 10 hours a week and has driven a 20%-plus increase in her income.
Similarly, Lindsey Gamble , vice president of creator strategy & innovation at IZEA, highlights a productivity trend. Creators are building their own searchable content hubs, feeding years of newsletters and old captions into an AI tool to surface through-lines they’d otherwise forget they’d already covered.
No matter how efficient these tools become, Buckner emphasizes, they’re not replacing what actually makes someone worth hiring. “I don’t think any of these tools are going to substantially replace depth of knowledge and expertise,” she says.
If AI hasn’t caught up to human expertise, the law hasn’t caught up to AI. “Law is so far behind, it’s never going to be able to catch up to the speed of technology,” says Buckner. “We’re still citing cases from like 1963.”
With many rules still unwritten, brands have started pushing the boundaries of what they can ask for. Buckner has started seeing a new kind of clause — brands willing to let creators use AI, on the condition that the creators hand over access to their prompts and processes. Her response is clear: “Immediately, no. That’s unnecessary access.”
In her view, the prompting process, not just the finished post or video, is where a creator’s actual thinking lives. Handing it over gives a brand insight into a creator’s mind that has nothing to do with the deliverable they paid for. Regardless of whether the law formally recognizes it yet, she suggests creators establish their own boundaries.
Gamble has seen the inverse version of this play out in creator contracts: brands banning AI use outright. One clause he recently encountered required that a creator not use any AI software, tools, or technologies without the brand’s prior written consent. He predicted that creators, not just brands, would eventually start writing their own AI-use clauses into agreements, protecting how their content and voice can be repurposed by brands using AI, not just the other way around.
Annie-Mai Hodge, founder of Girl Power Marketing (and also a HubSpot partner), sees a different platform-specific contradiction playing out. Social platforms are pushing AI tools directly into creators’ dashboards, she says, while simultaneously penalizing the content those same tools produce. “We are stuck in this incredibly frustrating paradox where platforms demand AI adoption but punish the output,” says Hodge. The result, she argues, is creators who are either too nervous to experiment with the tools they’re being handed, or too afraid to admit they already have.
Robinson has witnessed what happens when creators rely on AI without fully understanding the fine print. She points to a creator who partnered with one brand, then posted content for a direct competitor just two weeks later. That fell well within the exclusivity window most brand deals require — something Robinson knows firsthand from her own partnerships with the same agency.
She wonders, “Was that an AI problem that she didn’t actually read and comprehend, because she just sent it to AI and said, ‘negotiate for me’?”
On another note, the mere act of feeding a confidential contract into a public tool like ChatGPT, Robinson notes, can sometimes itself put a creator in breach, depending on how strict the brand’s legal team is.
This is precisely why Buckner is so passionate about the legal support she offers to creators. AI can help a creator understand what a term like “perpetuity” means, she says, but it can’t tell them how that term will actually play out in their specific circumstances. Connecting the definition to the real-life consequence, Buckner believes, is still a human job.
In many ways, AI has become the great equalizer. Gamble sees that case play out constantly in his work with creators. What once required a big budget is now available to anyone with a laptop and a subscription. “It gives them the tools that bigger creators have with teams and dedicated staff and more funds,” he says of emerging creators. Scripts, captions, rough cuts, carousels — the entire production pipeline that once required hired help now takes minutes.
The same tools that lower the barrier to entry are also flattening what comes out the other side. “If everyone’s using the same thing and doing the same thing, a lot of the content feels the same,” Gamble says. It’s a byproduct of thousands of creators prompting the same handful of AI tools in largely the same ways.
According to data from Lean In cited by Hodge, women are 22% less likely than men to be regular AI users at work, and 32% more likely to worry they’ll be seen as “cheating” if they use it. “While it’s my choice to keep AI out of my core workflow,” says Hodge, “we need to look at why women are conditioned to feel guilty for plugging it into their daily operations.”
Meanwhile, Hodge sees a different, more positive version of this play out in negotiations, where AI has actually started closing a different kind of gap around pay. Rate transparency has long been one of the creator economy’s biggest taboos, she says, and AI chatbots have made it easier for creators to find industry benchmarks. It might not get the brand to pay the creator more, but “it gives the creator more power and confidence to negotiate,” she adds.
If there was one word Robinson heard most at Cannes this year — even more than “AI” or “creators” — it was the word human. She reads it as a sign that even at a major marketing event, people still wanted to know a human was driving the work.
For Taylor, the answer is simple. “AI does not have feelings, it does not have emotion,” she says. “You can’t replace human connection.”
Gamble sees the cost of skipping that human step play out in real time, especially on LinkedIn. “Everyone’s writing sounds the same,” he says. “No one really has a voice, because everyone’s using the same thing.” His metaphor for what’s lost is that creativity is a muscle. The moment you stop using it, you lose it, the same way a body does when it stops training.
Gamble’s suggestion to creators is to protect that muscle, periodically writing, filming, or ideating without any tools at all, the way they did before AI existed. He also flags disclosure as a variable creators should watch closely — content that reads as AI-generated and undisclosed, he’s noticed, tends to get an immediate cold reception from audiences.
Richardson draws the same conclusion from the brand side. Raw, AI-generated animation has its place, she says, but when it comes to creator-led content specifically, she doesn’t see AI taking over. “People connect with human beings, and that won’t ever change.”
Hodge still reads every social media update herself each week, summarizing them in her own words, rather than automating the process. “Some people might think I’m mad for doing it that way,” she says, “but respectfully, ChatGPT and Claude can’t do it like I can.” Her advice to other creators: you don’t need to avoid the tools, you just need to be precise about where they belong. “If you are going to use it,” she says, “make it work harder for you.” In other words, it’ll never be you.

title: Ex-Googler Jeff Dean Explains Design Choices Behind Gemini via @sejournal, @martinibuster
content:
Jeff Dean recently explained the origins of Gemini, including the design philosophy behind it. Surprisingly, Gemini was lagging a bit until its coding abilities were improved, which subsequently improved the model’s reasoning ability.
Dean explains that the origin of Gemini was when he realized that there were multiple teams working separately toward the same goal. From the outside looking in, that seems like a silly approach, and that’s exactly the insight Dean had.
“So now looking back on the development of Gemini, what surprised you the most and what lessons from building Gemini do you think that you can share and can help shape the next generation of AI systems?”
“I think Gemini is really the culmination of a few earlier research projects, both within Legacy DeepMind and Google Brain and other parts of Google Research.
And at that time, we sort of realized that we were all converging to very similar kinds of directions, like training, trying to scale up the size of models we trained. We had some efforts, independent parallel efforts, on how do you make language models also be multimodal so they can understand images and so on.
And I wrote a one-page memo. I’m like, this is just silly. We should just all work together. Let’s combine our people and ideas and compute resources and train one model that is multimodal from the start that brings our best people together from across multiple research organizations within Google.
…And so we sort of saw a way to bring ourselves back in closer collaboration. And I think that’s been a really successful thing.”
We know that Gemini is multimodal, but what is less known is that this was a design effort from the very beginning. Dean explained that the goal for Gemini was to create a model that could understand audio, images, language, text, and other forms of information. But interestingly, it was when they trained it for coding that Gemini experienced a breakthrough improvement in reasoning.
“I think the focus on making the model multimodal from the beginning has been really, really good. You want the model that you’re gonna use for everything to understand text and language and code and images and videos and audio and other modalities besides.
So like we put a little bit of, say, LiDAR data in the training data so it at least knows that LiDAR data is a thing because that’s an important use case for, you know, further training of Gemini models. So that is important.
And that’s been, I think, a success of a decision we made at the very beginning to bring that through all the current Gemini models as well. …We wanted to make the model good at lots of things.
And so I think maybe our focus on making it amazing at coding was lagging a little bit and we realized that in our work to catch up on that.
And I think we have good efforts underway. But I think by focusing on that, you end up with a system that is able to really do a good job of reasoning and doing other kinds of tasks that needs to sort of work its way through breaking a complicated problem down into multiple sub-pieces and so on.
And so that’s a good– if you improve coding, you also tend to improve that capability in non-coding things.”
That’s actually super interesting because it shows how making the LLM expert in one thing leads to benefits in other areas. This is actually kind of similar to how humans become expert in things. Many centuries ago, a samurai sword master named Miyamoto Musashi encouraged learning arts and professions that are outside of the martial arts. He used carpentry as an example of how a master carpenter understands tools, planning, how to manage workers, and understands the structure of buildings and then maps those skills and insights back into the martial art of sword fighting.
Jeff Dean’s explanation about the origin of Gemini is useful because it gives users a better understanding of what Gemini is, creating an awareness of what is possible with Gemini when it’s considered as a multimodal model, not just a generative text model.
“So essentially, this is one thing that stands out about your career is that so many of these ideas, from MapReduce to MOE and so on, they actually took years before the broader community realized how important they would become.
But you had the Midas touch, and you had the special, really foresight to actually build and develop these ideas and systems and so on.
So I think many people in the audience would love to learn how do you do it?
How do you distinguish between technologies that are genuinely foundational and those are simply fashionable?
And what engineering principle that has remained surprisingly timeless throughout your career?
And also as AI shifts from models to increasingly autonomous agents, what new abstractions do you think we’ll need over the next few years and decades for our future?”
“I think I’ve been very lucky, maybe, as part of it. But I also think one of the things I try to do is keep track of a lot of different trends or research topics that the community is exploring.
I often tell students it’s better to skim 10 papers than to read one in detail, because you kind of then get 10 points in your cloud of what might be possible, or even skim 100 abstracts.
Because what you want to be able to do is connect important ideas that have not yet been connected.
And sometimes when you think about a hard problem, if you have some of these things that are now kind of vaguely starting to be possible in mind, that can help you kind of shape a full solution to a problem where instead of it seeming like seven unsolvable problems, you can squint at it and say, okay, well, these five things, I know there’s sort of vague work going on that seems important and might be able to address some of the things.
Then there’s two sort of additional things that I have no idea how to do. But if I work hard on them, I can imagine solving those.
And sometimes that’s super important to do the things that are incremental improvements to what we’re doing now, but you want to look for the things that are you know, maybe very different ways of doing things that might be possible or might be possible soon.
…I’ve done a bunch of things that have not worked out well too, so that’s also a good tip. Try lots of things that might not work. Some of them will.”
